doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Touring Japan with James Morrison and Rolf Harris
summary: Baker recalls the Tokyo expo tour with James Morrison and Rolf Harris, whose watercolours went to charity, and novelty Australian songs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah. I mean when we think of Australian music we probably think of, you know novelty songs, “Tie Me Kangaroo Down, Sport.”
Yeah, well, at one time that was true. I remember hearing that on the radio when I was young in the sixties. Rolf Harris. And actually I toured with Rolf Harris once.
No kidding? That’s a bit of trivia.

Yeah, in Japan. You might have heard of James Morrison? Okay, he’s a multi-talented instrumentalist who’s worked with Ray Brown and the Philip Morris Superband and gee, all sorts of guys. And he’s — wait a minute — can we cut there?
Yeah.
I just forgot what I was going to say.
You were talking about James Morrison and playing with Rolph Harris.
Rolf Harris. Okay. Sorry about that. Where shall I take it up?
Well, we were just — I was mentioning how we don’t have a very good conception of what goes on in Australia.
You want to start that again?
As far as music.
When we think of Australian music, we think of novelty songs. Like “Tie Me Kangaroo Down, Sport.”

Well I happened to tour Japan with this multi-instrumentalist, James Morrison. And it was the expo in Tokyo, and every country had a week to do their own thing, present their own music and their food. And Rolf Harris was on the bill with us, along with Roger Woodward the pianist, and opera stars and a few other people. And Rolf did “Tie Me Kangaroo Down,” and he played the wobble board, which was just a board — quite effective. And he did this thing where we played [sings] “Sakura” da da da da da you © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

know the Japanese theme. And he set out the front. And he’d do a watercolor, which was real good, and when we finished the tune, he finished the watercolor and signed it, and then proceeded to give it to these people in the front, for charity. And they’d auction it off and they’d get all this money. And he did this on every concert in Japan. He finished with a watercolor, and gave it to charity. So I thought that was a good thing to do. But I asked him about “Tie Me Kangaroo, Down” and he said, “Yeah, everybody thought that was the only Australian music, because it was the number one hit.”
Well there was also “My Boomerang Won’t Come Back.”
Oh, yeah, yeah. “I’ve practiced ‘till I was black in the face/my boomerang won’t come back.” You can’t even mention that though these days. They never play that on the radio anymore.
No, I guess not.
Oh, it’s politically very incorrect. But The Seekers, you know, they were Australian.
Oh, yeah?
And we heard them on the radio, and we didn’t know. No one ever said they were Australian. We thought they were English.
